From Pia Arke's exhibition *Arctic Hysteria*, Greenland's National Museum & Archives, Nuuk, 2010

**i.**
I inhabit my body. I stand here, before you. I am the very temperature of this room. I am unclothed in my nakedness; I am the light and shadow you perceive. I am more akin to others than to you. I possess a before and an after. I am myself, wholly and solely. My exterior and interior form an unbroken continuum. I am muscle, organ, fluid, bone. I am monumental. You alone perceive me.

**ii.**
I am not naked as I am, but naked as you behold me. I am transparent, nearly invisible. I occupy a time and a place. I am tribal, exotic. I am compelled always to bear objects. You are heroic. I am a museum unto myself, the narrative of my own becoming. I am a mirror in which you are reflected through the act of looking. At best, I echo you. You inscribe me. When you depart, I shall cease to exist.

**iii.**
I am a single point of consciousness. I am indifferent. I am unselfed, like a photogram. I am prehistoric, preceding all definition. Your body falls across me. I possess depth and luminescence. I am neither here nor there; I extend infinitely. I dwell within the lived world, light and dark shifting inside my head like the substance of dreams. I am camera obscura, the room itself. I both adore and resist.

# On Embodiment, Perception, and the Politics of Being Seen

The text under consideration offers a fragmented, multi-part meditation that resists easy synthesis—deliberately so. Its structure mirrors its subject matter: a self that is not singular but split, refracted through multiple lenses of perception, representation, and lived experience. Rather than presenting a linear argument, the work accumulates meaning through juxtaposition, allowing embodiment, identity, and visibility to circle one another in tension rather than resolution.

At the core of this meditation lies a fundamental distinction between two modes of existing. On one hand, there is the authentic, felt reality of bodily presence—captured in the declarative simplicity of "I am in my body." This is existence as immediate, sovereign, and self-evident, requiring no external validation. On the other hand, the text introduces a second, radically different mode of being: identity as it is *constructed* through an external, colonizing gaze. "I am naked as you see me" signals not vulnerability freely chosen, but exposure imposed—a self that only comes into being through the act of being looked at, categorized, and consumed by another's perception. The juxtaposition of these two phrases exposes the violence embedded in the gap between selfhood as lived and selfhood as observed.

This tension becomes explicitly political in the text's critique of exoticization and the objectification of Indigenous and tribal identities. Here, the subject is transformed into what the text chillingly calls a "complete museum"—a metaphor that captures the totalizing nature of colonial representation. To become a museum is to be simultaneously preserved and embalmed, put on display for consumption while stripped of narrative agency. The exhibits are curated, labeled, and interpreted not by the subject but by the very gaze that constructed them as "other." This critique speaks to a broader history in which tribal and Indigenous peoples have been rendered as artifacts—objects of fascination and study—rather than as subjects possessing the authority to write their own stories. The museum, in this sense, is not a neutral space of preservation but an active mechanism of control, where the colonized body becomes a text authored entirely by colonizing hands.

From this critique emerges one of the text's most devastating philosophical propositions: that visibility and existence are inextricably, perhaps parasitically, linked. The line "When you leave, I will no longer exist" crystallizes this anxiety, suggesting that the subject's very ontological status is contingent upon being witnessed by an external observer. This is not simply a comment on loneliness or the desire for connection—it points to something more insidious, a mode of being that has been so thoroughly colonized that it no longer trusts its own persistence outside the frame of another's attention. Existence becomes performative, sustained only through continuous external validation. The erasure threatened here is not just symbolic but total: the self, once unwitnessed, risks slipping into non-being entirely.

The final movement of the piece marks a significant tonal and conceptual shift, moving from the grounded, painful specifics of colonial critique into a more abstract, dreamlike register. The metaphor of the "camera obscura" is particularly rich here—an apparatus that captures and inverts light, producing an image that is both real and distorted, present and displaced. In comparing the self to this optical device, the text suggests a consciousness caught in paradox: one that both invites and resists the projections cast upon it. The camera obscura does not simply reflect what is shown to it; it transforms incoming light into inverted image, complicit in the very act of representation while also revealing the mechanics of that distortion. This final image suggests a kind of reclaimed agency—not a rejection of being seen, but an acknowledgment that the self can hold, refract, and ultimately expose the very act of being projected upon, turning the gaze back upon itself.

Together, these fragments form a powerful, if unresolved, exploration of what it means to exist within and against structures of external perception—embodying the profound difficulty of maintaining authentic selfhood in a world that persistently seeks to define, display, and dissolve the subject according to its own desires.

# Three Bodies, One Gaze: Reading Pia Arke's Poetic Triptych

Pia Arke's exhibition includes a three-part poetic meditation that functions less as a single unified statement than as a triptych of shifting perspectives, each panel offering a different relationship between the self who inhabits a body and the eye that observes it. The piece moves through grammatical and psychological registers—from "I" to "you" and back again—creating a destabilized sense of who is speaking, who is being spoken to, and who is being watched. This linguistic instability is not incidental; it is the mechanism through which Arke stages the central drama of the work: the way selfhood, particularly an Indigenous or otherwise marked selfhood, becomes contested territory between lived experience and external interpretation.

**The First Movement: Corporeal Presence**

The opening section grounds itself in the immediacy of the body—sweat, breath, the weight of limbs, the particular textures of skin and hair experienced from the inside. Here the speaker exists in what might be called an unmediated present tense, prior to any framing gaze. This is selfhood as it is lived rather than as it is seen: a consciousness fully coextensive with its physical form, unburdened by the need to signify anything beyond its own immediate sensation. The "I" of this section is whole, sovereign, and untranslated—existing for itself rather than for an audience.

**The Second Movement: The Fetishized Object**

The second section marks a rupture. The perspective shifts, often to a "you" that implicates an external viewer, and the body that was previously felt from within is now described as it appears to another—catalogued, admired, exoticized. This is the moment where colonial desire enters the text: the body becomes a site of fascination precisely because it is coded as "other," its features remarked upon not as lived particularities but as ethnographic curiosities. The language here often mimics the vocabulary of collection and display—the body is examined, appraised, made available for consumption by a gaze that carries with it centuries of colonial expectation about what an Indigenous or othered body should represent. This section captures the violence of objectification: the way desire and domination can become indistinguishable when the observer's interest is rooted in difference rather than recognition.

**The Third Movement: Abstraction and Timelessness**

The final section pulls back from both the intimacy of the first section and the scrutiny of the second, moving into a register that is more abstract, almost disembodied. Here the "I" becomes something closer to pure consciousness—untethered from specific physical markers, existing outside of clear temporal or spatial coordinates. This abstraction can be read two ways simultaneously: as a kind of escape or transcendence from the objectifying frame established in the second section, but also as the endpoint of that same process of objectification—the body having been so thoroughly transformed into symbol and artifact that it is no longer really a body at all, but an idea, a cultural sign, a timeless "Native" figure abstracted from any particular life.

**The Critical Arc**

Read together, the three sections trace a devastating progression: from full corporeal presence, to fetishized object, to abstracted and timeless consciousness. This arc illuminates something essential about how colonial and ethnographic frameworks operate on Indigenous and othered bodies—they do not simply look at these bodies but actively transform them, moving them through stages of increasing abstraction until the living, breathing person disappears entirely into cultural symbol. The exhibition's poem thus functions as both lament and critique: lament for the loss of embodied selfhood under the weight of the colonizing gaze, and critique of the very mechanisms—admiration, fascination, timeless mythologizing—that produce this loss. By shifting pronouns and perspectives throughout, Arke implicates the reader/viewer directly in this process, forcing an uncomfortable recognition of complicity in the very gaze the poem describes.

# Pia Arke and the Arctic Imagination

Pia Arke (1958–2007) was a Greenlandic-Danish artist whose work fundamentally reshaped conversations about Arctic identity, colonial history, and visual representation. Born in Scoresbysund (Ittoqqortoormiit) in East Greenland to a Danish father and Greenlandic mother, Arke occupied a unique position from which to examine the complex relationship between Denmark and its former colony.

Arke's practice spanned photography, installation, and written scholarship. She trained at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen, but her most significant contributions emerged from her deep engagement with Greenlandic history and the ways the Arctic had been visually constructed by outsiders—explorers, scientists, and colonial administrators.

One of her most celebrated techniques involved using a handmade camera obscura to photograph the Greenlandic landscape. These large-format images, often depicting dramatic fjords and icy terrain, deliberately echoed the aesthetic conventions of nineteenth-century polar expedition photography. Yet Arke's images subverted these conventions, reclaiming the landscape from a colonial gaze and asserting an Indigenous perspective on territory that had long been photographed, mapped, and possessed by others.

Her seminal work "Arctic Hysteria" (1996) exemplifies her critical approach. The piece referenced a historical psychological condition once diagnosed among Inuit women by European observers—a diagnosis now understood as reflecting colonial anxieties and misunderstandings rather than any genuine pathology. Arke's work interrogated how the Arctic and its peoples had been pathologized, exoticized, and studied through a distinctly colonial lens.

Beyond her artistic output, Arke was also a scholar and writer who explored postcolonial theory in relation to Greenland. Her book "Scoresbysundhistorier" (Scoresbysund Stories) combined personal narrative, historical documentation, and photography to explore her hometown's complicated colonial history, including the forced relocation of Inuit families from Northwest Greenland to establish the settlement.

Arke's legacy has grown substantially since her death, with retrospective exhibitions bringing renewed attention to her pioneering exploration of Arctic identity. Her work remains essential for understanding how the region has been represented, misrepresented, and reclaimed—offering a crucial counter-narrative to purely European or American framings of polar exploration and Arctic life. Today, she is recognized as a foundational figure in Indigenous Arctic art and postcolonial visual studies, having opened pathways for subsequent generations of Greenlandic and Indigenous artists to engage critically with questions of representation, territory, and identity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a three-part prose poem in the voice of the body as subject and object, inspired by Pia Arke's "Arctic Hysteria" exhibition, exploring nakedness, the gaze, and colonial representation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Arctic Hysteria: Three Movements

## I. Skin as Territory

I crawl across the photograph of my own country and my body becomes the paper it burns into. This is what they wanted—me on all fours, naked, moving across an image of a place that was supposed to be empty before they arrived to fill it with their looking. I am the fill. I am the proof of emptiness and its correction.

The camera does not ask permission. It has never asked permission. It arrives already knowing what it will find: a body to place against the ice, a body that is the ice's opposite and therefore its meaning. Cold needs warm flesh to prove it is cold. Wilderness needs a woman crawling through it to prove it is wilderness and not simply home.

I burn the paper landscape beneath my belly, my knees, the soft undersides of my arms. Where my body touches image, image blisters. This is not metaphor. This is the actual heat of being seen becoming the actual damage of the seen thing. Skin remembers every gaze as a small weather system, a front moving through, leaving frost-bright patches where something froze and did not thaw correctly.

They called it hysteria, this wandering of the womb, this body that would not stay still under observation, that insisted on producing its own meanings faster than they could be catalogued. Arctic hysteria: the diagnosis for those who scream in a language the doctors have already decided is symptom, not speech.

## II. The Body Photographed, The Body Photographing

I stand naked before the lens I am also holding. This is the trick no one taught them to see: that a woman can be both the held and the holding, both specimen and scientist, both the one who freezes in the image and the one who releases the shutter.

My father was half of this country and half of that one, and I am made of the same fracture, the same doubled seeing. I know what the anthropologist wants before he asks—wants the fur, the ice-cave mouth, the primitive nipple pointed toward his understanding like a compass toward a north he has already named. I give it to him. I give it to him and then I turn the photograph over and write on the back: *this was performed. this was a performance of your wanting.*

Nakedness is not the absence of clothing. Nakedness is the presence of every eye that has decided what my body means before my body has finished happening. I wear their theories like a second skin, itchy, imported, never quite fitting the actual weather of my actual flesh.

But here is what they did not photograph: the body getting dressed afterward. The body walking home through snow that belongs to no one's metaphor. The body eating dinner, laughing with a mouth that is not, in that moment, a specimen of anything. This body exceeds the image every single time. This is the secret hysteria—not that I cannot be contained, but that containment was always a lie the frame told about itself.

## III. What the Archive Cannot Hold

Call it repatriation: I take my grandmother's face back from the ethnographic photograph where it has been living as evidence. I take the bare shoulders, the steady eyes that refuse to perform the fear the caption wants. I take them home to a body that is mine, that is hers, that is the long unbroken line of women photographed as *before* so that someone else could stand as *after*, as *progress*, as *arrival*.

The gaze wanted a body without history, a nakedness that meant only nature, only ice, only the blank page that Denmark could write itself onto like a flag planted in snow. But my body has a history. My body is an archive that keeps producing documents the colonial record did not authorize—laughter, refusal, the specific weather of an actual life lived north of their imagination.

I am tired of being the landscape.
I am tired of being the ice that proves their warmth,
the wilderness that proves their civilization,
the naked body that proves their clothed authority.

So I photograph myself photographing them looking. I place my own bare skin against my own bare land and let the burning be mutual, let the damage run both directions, let the paper remember that it was never empty, that something was always living here, underneath the frost of their attention, keeping its own warm and complicated blood.

This is not hysteria.
This is the body finally speaking
in the only language
that was always its own.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you create an experimental art-critical text structured in three numbered sections (i, ii, iii) responding to Pia Arke's work, using repeated "I am" statements that shift from selfhood to being seen/objectified to something more abstract and photographic?
counterfactuals.output:
# Territories of the Skin

## i.

I am standing in Nuugaarsuk where my mother stood.
I am the daughter of a Danish father and a Greenlandic mother, and this sentence has already been used against me.
I am not an ethnographic subject.
I am not going to apologize for the camera in my hands.
I am the granddaughter of someone who was measured, photographed, catalogued.
I am aware that this awareness does not free me.
I am trying to stand in two places at once: behind the lens and in front of it.
I am the pinhole. I am the light that enters through the wound.

## ii.

I am being looked at.
I am being looked at by an archive that predates my birth.
I am the "type," the "specimen," the "half-breed" — words that arrive before I do, that furnish the room before I enter it.
I am composed, in the old sense: arranged, ordered, made to sit still.
I am a body the colonial eye already knows how to read.
I am asked to perform Greenland. I am asked to perform Denmark. I am asked which one is more true.
I am reproduced — in the photographic sense, in the imperial sense.
I am the negative someone else developed.
I am, in this image, already gone.

## iii.

I am the camera obscura built from a cardboard box and the shape of a room in Nuuk.
I am an aperture, not an answer.
I am the slow accumulation of light on a surface that cannot lie flat.
I am the landscape photographing itself through me.
I am neither figure nor ground but the membrane between them.
I am underexposed history, overexposed geography.
I am a fjord standing in for a mouth, a mouth standing in for a nation, a nation that will not resolve into a single print.
I am not a metaphor. I am the failure of metaphor to hold.
I am what remains when the shutter closes and the story refuses to develop as expected.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I'm writing a catalog essay for a Greenlandic photography exhibition—help me draft a poetic meditation on the body, the colonizer's gaze, and camera obscura, referencing Pia Arke's Arctic Hysteria at Nuuk's National Museum.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Skin of the Image: A Meditation for the Arctic Body

*Draft for catalog essay*

---

There is a room in Nuuk where a woman crawls across a photograph of her own homeland, and the sound she makes is not quite pain, not quite laughter, but something older than both—hysteria as etymology, as womb-word, as the body's refusal to hold still under the weight of being *seen*.

Pia Arke understood this. In *Arctic Hysteria* (1996), she rephotographed her father's landscape images—Nuugaarsuk, the terrain of her own childhood—by projecting them onto a screen and crawling naked across their surface, filming herself in the act. The camera obscura made literal: a body inside the darkroom of empire, moving through light that was never neutral, never simply *there*. The gaze that mapped her homeland becomes a surface she must physically inhabit, must scrape her skin against, must reclaim through friction.

This is what colonial photography does and undoes: it fixes a land, a people, a body, into an image that can be owned, catalogued, carried home to Copenhagen in a leather satchel. The Greenlandic body becomes specimen, becomes ethnographic evidence, becomes *before* in some Danish *after*. The camera obscura—that ancient device, that room of inverted light—is not innocent. It is the eye of the empire learning to see, and what it sees, it takes.

But Arke's crawling body refuses the taking. She inserts herself between the lens and the land, becomes obstruction, becomes the grain in the machine. Her nakedness is not the nakedness offered up to ethnography's cold catalog—it is armor, it is defiance, it is the body saying: *I will not be your evidence. I will be my own instrument.*

---

The pinhole is small. The world outside is vast, is blinding, is too much light to bear directly—so we build small dark rooms, we let the world enter upside down, inverted, manageable. This is how the colonizer learned to hold the Arctic in his palm: through diminishment, through image-making that shrank glaciers into postcards, shrank women into "Eskimo Venus" figures for European curiosity cabinets.

Greenlandic photographers today work inside that same optical inheritance, but they have learned to turn the aperture inward. What if the darkroom is not a chamber of capture but a chamber of return? What if the body, once fixed as specimen, becomes instead the *instrument*—the very device through which new light enters, is processed, is given back transformed?

---

To photograph the Arctic body now is to work in the residue of Arke's gesture: every image must reckon with the archive that came before, the drawers of glass plates in Danish museums, the scientific expeditions that measured skulls and catalogued "types." The camera in Greenlandic hands today is not innocent of this history—it cannot be—but it can be *haunted* correctly, can carry the weight of that history as knowledge rather than erasure.

The body in these photographs is not offered for consumption. It is not "before" awaiting a colonial "after." It exists in its own duration, its own light—Arctic light, which does not behave as European light behaves, which in summer refuses to set, which in winter teaches the eye to find color in what looks, from outside, like only darkness, only white, only absence.

---

Arke called her practice a form of "re-appropriation"—not reclaiming a lost authenticity, for she knew there was no pure Greenlandic image to return to, no innocence before the camera arrived. Instead: a working-*through*, a body that crawls across the old projections and in crawling, changes them. The scratch marks remain. The hybridity remains. This is not a wound to be healed but a text to be read, a palimpsest where empire's image and Indigenous body exist now in the same frame, contaminating and complicating each other.

This is the inheritance these photographers carry into Nuuk's museum walls: not the fantasy of an image untouched by history, but the harder, more honest work of making pictures that know exactly what pictures have done, and choose, anyway, to keep making them—differently.

---

*[This is a working draft—happy to adjust tone, expand specific sections, add more concrete visual/artist references, or tighten the language further depending on your exhibition's specific curatorial angle.]*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented, first-person text in three parts that moves from embodied presence, to being exoticized/tribalized under an outsider's gaze, to a final dissolution into light, image, and the mechanics of photography.
counterfactuals.output:
**I.**

Dust first. Always dust, rising to meet the arch of my foot before the foot arrives. My mother's hands smelled of onion and river water. I knew the world by weight — the weight of a clay pot on my head, the weight of my own hip against the doorframe at dusk.

Skin: warm. Skin: known. Skin that itched at the shoulder where the strap cut in, skin that remembered every field it had bent over.

Sound of goats. Sound of someone singing off-key three houses down. I was not thinking of myself as a body then. I was simply *in* it — breath moving, blood moving, the small ache in the left knee from kneeling too long at the mortar.

There was a smell of woodsmoke that meant evening. There was a taste — sour milk, millet — that meant home, that meant nothing else, that did not yet mean *authentic.*

I laughed with my mouth open. No one was counting my teeth.

**II.**

Then the man came with the box.

He said *fascinating.* He said *untouched.* He said, lowering his voice as if in a museum, *this is how they used to live everywhere.*

I became "they." I became "used to."

He asked me to stand still, to stand *natural,* which meant: stand as I imagine you standing when no one is looking, except now someone is looking, so stand as the someone imagines the no-one would.

My scarf became "traditional dress." My scar became "tribal marking." My grandmother's name for me — small bird, the one who cries at thunder — became "native name, meaning unclear."

He circled. He crouched low, lens first, as though approaching an animal that might startle.

I held my child on my hip the way I always held her. He said *hold her like that, yes, don't look at me, look past me, look like you're looking at the horizon of your ancestors.*

There was no horizon of my ancestors. There was a fence, and beyond the fence, his truck.

I felt my body arrange itself into a shape it did not choose. I felt the word *timeless* pressed onto me like a stamp, flattening whatever hour it actually was — Tuesday, hot, my knee still aching.

**III.**

Click.

And there — light through glass, upside down, correcting itself only inside the dark chamber no one else enters.

I am no longer kneeling at the mortar. I am a value of grey. I am 1/125th of a second, f/8, the sun slightly behind him so my face falls into shadow, so the shadow reads as "mystery," so the mystery sells.

Silver halide remembers what I no longer have to. Grain stands in for skin. My laugh, unphotographed, does not exist; my stillness, photographed, becomes the only fact of me.

Someone will caption this. Someone will not ask my name.

I flatten into paper. I flatten into paper the way dust flattens into footprints, the way a life flattens into a single chosen instant — chosen not by me, developed not by me, fixed in chemical bath, hung in a frame, called *timeless,* called *hers,* called nothing at all —

just light,
just the mechanism that caught it,
just the shutter's small mercy of closing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental piece exploring postcolonial identity and photographic representation, using anaphora ("I am...") across three shifting perspectives—self, other's projection, and abstract image/apparatus—in the spirit of Pia Arke's Arctic Hysteria.
counterfactuals.output:
# Three Exposures
*after Pia Arke*

---

## I. The Emulsion

I am the one who develops in darkness and does not yet know my own contours.

I am the girl in Nuugaarsuk who crawled naked across the photograph of her own coastline, my knees leaving no print in the paper, my skin the only negative that mattered.

I am half the archive and half the hand that built it — my mother's tongue folding into my father's grammar until I speak in the seam between them.

I am the fjord before anyone named it a fjord, before the ice became a word in someone else's dictionary of ice-words.

I am not the girl in the photograph. I am the photograph's shadow, standing just outside the frame, asking to be let in on my own terms or not at all.

I am the child who learned that home is a darkroom — you enter it blind, and wait, and something of you rises up out of the chemical bath, but it is never quite you.

---

## II. The Specimen

I am what the caption says I am.

I am *Eskimo woman, standing*, filed under 1883, drawer four, beside the walrus tusks and the maps that got the coastline wrong on purpose.

I am the body the anthropologist measured with calipers, translated into millimeters of skull, into a table of comparative data, into evidence for a theory that needed me to be simple.

I am the studio backdrop of painted ice — false glacier, false wind — because the real Arctic would not hold still long enough for the exposure.

I am the woman they called hysterical because grief, in my language, had no correct posture for the camera.

I am reproduced in a book still sold in the gift shop of the museum that owns my great-grandmother's likeness and will not say her name.

I am the "before" in someone's civilizing photograph, and there is no "after" — the after was never taken, or it was taken and marked *unsuitable for the collection.*

---

## III. The Aperture

I am the box with a hole in it. I am the hole.

I am the camera obscura built inside a turf hut, the whole cold sky inverted and thrown trembling onto a wall of stretched skin.

I am the mechanism, not the message — I do not choose what enters me, only how long I hold the light before I close.

I am the shutter's small violence, repeated, repeated, until repetition becomes a kind of authorship.

I am the lens that cannot apologize for what it was built to do, but can be turned, can be pried from its housing, can be re-mounted by different hands, pointed back.

I am the negative no one has printed yet — still reversible, still undecided, dark where the archive is light and light where the archive insists on dark.

I am, in the end, only ever partly developed: one image bleeding into the next, self and specimen and shutter refusing to resolve into a single, exposed, and finished print.
